n: The Bible opens by declaring that everything begins with God. Latter-day Saint scripture adds that God worked through His Son, and that “created” here means organizing existing matter rather than making something out of nothing.

f.g: Hebrew bara’ — to shape or form; used in the Bible only of God’s work. Abraham 4:1 renders it “organized and formed.”

n: Before God’s ordering work, the earth was shapeless, empty, and dark, covered by deep waters. Yet the Spirit of God was already present, hovering over it like a bird over its nest, ready to bring forth life.

f.g: Hebrew tohu wa-bohu — formless and empty. Days 1–3 give the earth form; days 4–6 fill it.
Hebrew raḥaf — to hover or brood, as a bird over its young (compare Deuteronomy 32:11).

n: God simply speaks, and light appears. This shows the power of His word. Christians have long seen a link to Jesus Christ, who is called the Word and the Light of the world.

God looks at His work and calls it good, a refrain repeated throughout the chapter. Separating light from darkness is the first of several acts of dividing and ordering that turn chaos into a home for life.

f.g: Separating and ordering is a key theme: light from darkness, waters from waters, sea from land.

n: Naming something showed authority over it. The Hebrew day begins at evening, which is why the text says “evening and morning.” Latter-day Saint scripture treats each creative “day” as a period of time rather than necessarily 24 hours.

f.g: Abraham 4:5 calls it “the first, or the beginning, of that which they called day and night”; the Abraham account speaks of creative “times.”

n: On the second day God makes an expanse, the sky, which separates waters above from waters below. To ancient eyes the sky looked like a great dome holding back rain clouds.

f.g: Hebrew raqiaʿ — something beaten or spread out; an expanse. Abraham 4:6 uses “expanse.”

n: The command is carried out exactly as spoken. “It was so” stresses that God’s word is always fulfilled. In the Abraham account, the Gods watch “until they obeyed,” showing creation responding to divine direction.

God names the expanse “Heaven,” meaning the sky. Notably, the second day is the only one where the text does not call the work “good”—many readers think the waters’ work was not finished until day three.

f.g: Here the visible sky, not the dwelling place of God.

n: On the third day the waters gather into one place and dry ground appears. A world fit for plants, animals, and people is being prepared step by step.
God names the land and seas and declares them good. The land is now ready to bear life, and God’s approval is stamped on it.

f.g: Hebrew yammim — the great waters, which ancient peoples often feared; here they are simply part of God’s ordered world.

n: God commands the earth to produce plants. Each one carries its own seed and reproduces “after his kind,” a built-in order that lets life continue and multiply on its own.

f.g: “His” is older English for “its.” Each kind reproduces according to its own pattern.

n: The earth obeys and becomes green with life. Seed-bearing plants and fruit trees will later feed both animals and people, showing God’s care in providing for His children before they arrive.

f.g: Plants in general, especially grain and vegetables—not just seasonings.

n: The third day closes. It contained two creative acts: forming dry land and clothing it with plants.

f.g: Days 1–3 create spaces (light, sky and sea, land); days 4–6 fill those spaces.

n: On the fourth day God places lights in the sky. They mark time—signs, seasons, days, and years—which later governs Israel’s calendar of feasts and sacred days.

f.g: Hebrew moʿadim — appointed times, the same word used for Israel’s holy festivals.

n: These lights have a practical purpose: to shine on the earth. Everything in creation is aimed at making the earth a good place for life.

f.w: to give light upon the earth

n: God makes the sun and moon, here called simply the greater and lesser lights, and almost in passing, the stars. Many neighboring peoples worshipped these bodies; Genesis presents them as God’s creations, not gods.
God sets the lights in their place in the sky. Their job is to serve the earth by giving light.

f.g: Placed or appointed—the lights have positions and roles assigned by God.

n: The sun and moon “rule” day and night, but only as servants doing what God assigned. Their ordered motion reflects God’s orderly creation.
The fourth day ends with the heavens now furnished with lights.

f.g: Day four fills the space made on day one (light and darkness).

n: On the fifth day the waters swarm with life and birds fill the sky. Life now moves and breathes, filling the spaces made on day two.

f.g: Swarming creatures—things that teem in great numbers.

n: God creates sea creatures large and small and every kind of bird. The great sea creatures, feared by ancient peoples as monsters, are shown to be simply part of God’s good creation.

f.g: Hebrew tannin — great sea creatures or sea monsters, not only whales.

n: God blesses the creatures to multiply. This is the first blessing in the Bible, and it is a blessing of life and increase.
The fifth day closes with sea and sky full of living things.

f.g: Day five fills the spaces separated on day two (waters below, sky above).

n: On the sixth day the land brings forth animals—livestock, small creeping creatures, and wild animals—each reproducing according to its kind.

f.g: In KJV English, domestic animals and livestock in general.

n: God makes every kind of land animal and approves of it. The stage is now set for the crowning act of creation.

f.g: Small ground creatures—insects, reptiles, and the like.

n: The tone changes: God speaks with others—“Let us.” Latter-day Saints understand this as the Father speaking with His Son and other heavenly beings. Humans are made in God’s image and given care of the earth.

f.w: in our image, after our likeness

f.g: Responsible stewardship—ruling as God would rule, with care (compare D&C 104:13-17).

n: The poetic repetition emphasizes the point: men and women alike are created in God’s image. Both sexes together reflect the divine. Latter-day Saints teach that we are literally spirit children of Heavenly Parents.

f.w: male and female created he them

n: God blesses the first man and woman and gives them their first commandment: have children and care for the earth. Family and stewardship are woven into human purpose from the start.

f.g: Here simply “fill”—not “refill.”
To bring under control and make productive; to cultivate.

n: God provides food for humanity: seed-bearing plants and fruit. He is a generous Father who prepares for His children’s needs.

f.g: In KJV English, “meat” means food of any kind, not just animal flesh.

n: Animals, too, receive green plants for food. The picture is of a peaceful world where every creature is provided for.
God surveys everything and declares it “very good”—the only time this stronger phrase appears. The creation, including the human body, is good. This ends the sixth day.
